title: Medical Student Experiences in a 4-Week Immersive Disability Elective: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Knowledge and Attitudes
content: Despite growing recognition of health disparities affecting people with disabilities (PWD), most medical schools provide limited disability-specific training, and evidence on optimal curricular design is limited. This study evaluated the impact of a four-week, immersive, post-clerkship disability elective course on medical students' attitudes and knowledge. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we assessed 64 students across nine cohorts. Attitudes were measured with the Medical Student Attitudes toward Persons with Disabilities Scale (MSA-PWD) administered pre- and post-course (n = 49 matched pairs); knowledge was assessed via end-of-course examinations and a barrier-identification essay exercise. End-of-course debrief transcripts underwent directed content analysis. Students showed significant improvement across all four MSA-PWD factors and the total score (median 50.0 to 58.0, p &lt; 0.001), with 95.9% improving relative to baseline. Exam performance was strong (mean 75.3%), though the essay exercise revealed variable ability to identify communication and attitudinal barriers across disability types, particularly for intellectual/developmental conditions. Qualitative findings linked attitudinal gains to structured community immersion and engagement with disabled faculty. In conclusion, an immersive, community-engaged disability elective can meaningfully improve medical student attitudes and support applied disability knowledge, underscoring the value of longitudinal curricular integration.
